description: Take the Petronas Towers apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of Cesar Pelli's twin supertalls: 88 floors, 451.9 meters, and the double-decker skybridge that made them the world's tallest buildings.

hotspots.text: The double-decker skybridge joins the towers at levels 41 and 42: 58.4 meters long, 170 meters above the street, weighing 750 tons. It is not rigidly fixed to either tower, so it can move independently in high wind, and it doubles as a fire escape.
hotspots.title: The skybridge

hotspots.text: The stainless steel spire of Tower 1 completes the architectural height of 451.9 meters (1,483 ft). It was the spires, not the roofs, that made these the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004.
hotspots.title: The spire

hotspots.text: Each tower's floor plan is an eight-pointed star made of two interlocking squares, an Islamic geometric motif standing for unity, harmony, stability and rationality. The shafts taper in setbacks as they rise.
hotspots.title: The eight-pointed star

hotspots.text: The public observation deck sits on level 86 at 370 meters, below the top floor at 375 meters. The skybridge is the other visitor experience, at half the height.
hotspots.title: The observation deck

hotspots.text: Each tower stands on a 4.5-meter-thick concrete raft over 104 barrette piles driven 60 to 115 meters deep, among the deepest foundations in the world. The site was a former horse race track.
hotspots.title: The foundations

hotspots.text: The stiff central concrete core carries the lifts, stairs and services and takes more than half the wind's overturning load: the inner tube of the tube-in-tube structure. Each tower has 29 double-deck high-speed passenger lifts.
hotspots.title: The lift core

hotspots.text: Islamic geometric patterning runs through the whole design, from the star plan to the stainless steel and glass facade screens: 65,000 square meters of steel and 77,000 of glass.
hotspots.title: The Islamic facade

intro: Two identical towers, 451.9 meters of stainless steel and glass, joined halfway up by a bridge that floats between them. This is how Kuala Lumpur bought itself a place on the world skyline.
page_title: Petronas Towers: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body:
In 1992 Malaysia set out to announce its arrival as a modern economy, and it chose an Argentine architect to do it. Cesar Pelli's design for the Petronas Towers wrapped a very Islamic idea, the eight-pointed star of two interlocking squares, around a very American one, the supertall office tower. The star stands in Islamic geometry for unity, harmony, stability and rationality, and it gives the towers their unmistakable faceted silhouette.

Construction ran from 1993 to 1996 on the site of a former horse race track, at a cost of US$1.6 billion. Each tower has 88 floors, five of them underground. The architectural height is 451.9 meters, measured to the stainless steel spires, and that measurement mattered: from their completion in 1998 until Taipei 101 passed them in 2004, they were the tallest buildings in the world. They remain the tallest twin towers on earth. The structure is tube-in-tube: a stiff central concrete core taking the lifts and services, wrapped in a perimeter frame, founded on a 4.5-meter raft over 104 barrette piles up to 115 meters deep.
sections.heading: The race for the sky

sections.body:
What makes the Petronas Towers different from every other pair of tall buildings is the skybridge. At levels 41 and 42, 170 meters above the street, a double-decker bridge 58.4 meters long links the two towers. It weighs 750 tons and it is deliberately not rigidly attached to either tower: in high wind the bridge can move independently while the towers sway around it.

The bridge is also a second way out. In a fire or emergency it serves as an escape route from one tower to the other, which is why a bridge that looks like pure architectural theater is also a piece of life-safety engineering. Visitors walk it today as the towers' signature experience, halfway between the street and the level 86 observation deck at 370 meters.
sections.heading: A bridge between giants

sections.body:
The towers' most famous screen appearance is also their most brazen. In Entrapment (1999), Sean Connery and Catherine Zeta-Jones play thieves planning to steal $8 billion from the fictional International Clearance Bank, headquartered in the North Tower. The climax runs through the towers and across the skybridge, and the production filmed on location in Kuala Lumpur, putting the barely finished towers in front of a global audience the year they opened.

Seventeen years later the towers got the disaster-movie treatment. The trailer for Independence Day: Resurgence (2016) showed the Petronas Towers torn from the ground by the aliens' gravity weapon and dropped onto London, collapsing across Tower Bridge and into the Thames. Malaysian audiences noticed immediately: the national landmark, demolished for a trailer beat, with Jeff Goldblum's character sighing, "They like to get the landmarks."

Between fiction and reality, the towers have also been climbed for real. In 2009 the French urban climber Alain Robert, the "Spider-Man" of skyscrapers, scaled one of the towers free-climbing to the top at 451.9 meters, adding the building to his long list of the world's tallest ascents.

timeline.text: Groundbreaking for the Petronas Towers on a former horse race track in Kuala Lumpur.
Construction of the twin towers to Cesar Pelli's design; Tower 1 by Hazama, Tower 2 by Samsung C&T.
The towers become the tallest buildings in the world at 451.9 meters.
Entrapment is released, with its climax set at the towers.
The towers are officially opened by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad.
Taipei 101 surpasses them; they remain the world's tallest twin towers.
Alain Robert free-climbs one of the towers to its 451.9-meter top.
The Independence Day: Resurgence trailer shows the towers collapsing onto London.
